SSP_LABOUR_REFORM.label: Supply-side policy: reforming the labour market (e.g. trade union reform, minimum wage changes)

SSP_SKILLS.label: Supply-side policy: improving skills and quality of the labour force (education/training)

stages.name: Supply-side policies
stages.title: Supply-side policies
stages.sub: Distinguish market-based from interventionist supply-side policies and identify examples of each.

steps.q: A government cuts income tax so workers keep more of each extra pound they earn, then leaves them to decide how much to work. Is the government directing what happens next, or leaving the outcome to individual choices?
steps.hint: Once the tax is cut, who decides how much extra effort to put in?

steps.q: A government instead passes a law forcing firms to retrain all workers over 50. Is that outcome left to individual choices, or is it imposed directly by the state?
steps.hint: Can firms simply choose not to retrain anyone here?

steps.q: Tax cuts rely on people responding to changed incentives, while a retraining law simply orders firms to act. Are these two approaches to boosting an economy's output the same kind of policy, or two different kinds?
steps.wrong: The same kind, just different examples
steps.hint: One removes barriers and lets choices happen, the other tells firms what to do.

steps.q: A government cuts the top rate of income tax and reduces unemployment benefits, hoping people work longer hours and job-seekers take work sooner. Is this changing what people are allowed to do, or changing what it is worth their while to do?
steps.right: Changing what it is worth their while to do
steps.wrong: Changing what people are allowed to do
steps.hint: Nobody is forced to work more; they just keep more money if they do.

steps.prompt: Drag and drop the 4 key terms in the order they build on each other.

steps.q: A government sells off a state-owned railway and removes rules that stopped new airlines entering routes. Does this order firms to behave a certain way, or open the market up so more firms compete for customers?
steps.right: Opens the market up to more competing firms
steps.wrong: Orders firms to behave a certain way
steps.hint: New firms can now enter and challenge existing ones on price and quality.

steps.q: A government passes laws limiting trade unions' power to call strikes and changes the rules on the minimum wage. Does this change how easily firms can hire, fire and set pay, or does it change how skilled workers are?
steps.right: Changes how easily firms can hire, fire and set pay
steps.hint: Strikes and pay-setting rules affect the flexibility of employing people, not their training.

steps.q: A government funds more apprenticeships and technical college places so workers can do more advanced, higher-value jobs. Does this change the rules employers must follow, or change what workers are capable of doing?
steps.right: Changes what workers are capable of doing
steps.wrong: Changes the rules employers must follow
steps.hint: Apprenticeships build ability rather than changing hiring laws.
